title: This vs That
description: A head-to-head voting app where users compare two items and see how everyone else voted.

caseStudy.problem: People debate preferences endlessly with no easy way to settle it or see how others voted.
caseStudy.approach: Wireframed a swipe-first voting flow, then built a real-time leaderboard with cached vote aggregation.
caseStudy.outcome: Shipped an authenticated, mobile-friendly voting app with social sharing and image hosting via Cloudinary.
caseStudy.design: Built a bold, high-contrast matchup screen so the two options carry all the visual weight. Type and color do the work of the interface — the vote itself is the only affordance on screen.
caseStudy.wireframing: Started with paper sketches of the swipe gesture, then moved to low-fidelity frames to test how quickly a user could get from landing to first vote. Cut the onboarding step entirely once testing showed it stalled people.
caseStudy.assets: Matchup imagery is uploaded through Cloudinary with on-the-fly transforms, so a single source image serves every breakpoint. The logo mark and result-share cards were built in Figma and exported as SVG.

title: Game Gem
description: A discovery tool that surfaces new video games from a plain-language description of what you feel like playing.

caseStudy.problem: Game catalogs are searchable by genre and tag, but not by the fuzzy way people actually describe what they want to play next.
caseStudy.approach: Put an LLM in front of the IGDB catalog: free-text intent is turned into structured query parameters, then results are re-ranked and summarized. Inference runs on Lambda so cost scales with real usage.
caseStudy.outcome: Shipped a natural-language search that returns a short, explained shortlist instead of an unranked result grid — and stays responsive by caching the expensive IGDB lookups.
caseStudy.design: Leaned on cover art as the primary visual, with a restrained shell around it so the artwork carries the page. Results are cards, not rows, because the box art is the fastest signal a player reads.
caseStudy.wireframing: Mapped the flow from a single search field to a result set to a detail view, deliberately keeping it to three screens. Early frames tested whether users trusted an AI-written recommendation blurb — they did, provided the source data stayed visible alongside it.
caseStudy.assets: Cover art and screenshots come straight from the IGDB API rather than being hosted locally. Iconography and empty-state illustrations were drawn in Figma to match the app's rounded, arcade-adjacent tone.

title: Tripr
description: A trip planner that turns a list of stops into a mapped, bookable itinerary.

caseStudy.problem: Planning a multi-stop trip means juggling a map in one tab, booking sites in another, and a notes app holding it together.
caseStudy.approach: Built the itinerary and the map as one view — editing the list reorders the route, and dragging the route reorders the list. A .NET API keeps the itinerary authoritative so both surfaces stay in sync.
caseStudy.outcome: Shipped a planner where the route, the stops, and the bookings live in a single view, with Mapbox handling geocoding and directions.
caseStudy.design: The map is the canvas and the itinerary is a panel over it, so the trip always reads geographically first. Stop markers are numbered and color-coded by day to make a long route legible at a glance.
caseStudy.wireframing: Wireframed the split between map and list at several ratios before settling on an overlay panel that collapses — on a phone, the map is what people want to see, and the list is what they want to edit.
caseStudy.assets: Map styling is a custom Mapbox Studio theme tuned to the site's palette rather than a stock basemap. Marker and category icons were built as a small SVG set so they stay crisp at every zoom level.
